THOUGHT: A 13-year-old male presents with 2 months of progressive left leg pain, initially misattributed to “growing pains” but now severe enough to disrupt sleep. The temporal association with a baseball impact one week prior raises concern for trauma-triggered symptom onset—but the persistence and progression beyond expected soft-tissue injury healing (which typically resolves in days to 2 weeks) strongly suggest an underlying pathological process unmasked or exacerbated by trauma. Physical exam reveals focal tenderness over the mid-femur without current inflammation (no erythema/swelling), arguing against acute cellulitis or uncomplicated muscle contusion. Laboratory findings show marked leukocytosis (WBC 21,000/μL) and elevated ESR (68 mm/h), indicating systemic inflammation or malignancy—neither typical of benign growing pains nor simple trauma. The X-ray finding of *multiple lytic lesions in the mid-femur with laminated (‘onion-skin’) periosteal new bone formation* is highly characteristic of aggressive bone pathology. While infection (e.g., osteomyelitis) can cause lytic lesions and periosteal reaction, multiple discrete lytic foci with layered periosteal reaction are atypical for pyogenic osteomyelitis (which usually shows a single dominant focus with ill-defined bone destruction and less organized periosteal reaction). In contrast, this radiographic pattern—especially with associated systemic inflammatory markers and persistent pain—is classic for *Ewing sarcoma*, the second most common primary malignant bone tumor in adolescents. Critically, the biopsy reveals *small round blue cells*, which is the hallmark histopathological appearance of Ewing sarcoma (as well as other small round blue cell tumors like lymphoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, or neuroblastoma—but those are far less likely to present as multifocal lytic femoral lesions with periosteal reaction in this age group and anatomical location). Ewing sarcoma commonly arises in the diaphysis/metaphysis of long bones (e.g., femur), presents with pain ± swelling, often has constitutional symptoms (though not yet reported here), and may be preceded by minor trauma that draws attention to an already symptomatic lesion. The absence of fever does not exclude malignancy; systemic symptoms can be subtle early on. Other considerations—such as Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) or leukemia—can cause lytic lesions, but LCH typically presents with solitary (not multiple) lesions and lacks prominent layered periosteal reaction; leukemia more commonly causes diffuse bone marrow infiltration with nonspecific pain and cytopenias (here, Hb and platelets are normal, WBC is elevated but not blast-laden—no peripheral smear provided, but biopsy is definitive). The combination of age, location, radiographic features (multifocal lysis + onion-skin periostitis), lab abnormalities (inflammatory markers), and biopsy showing small round blue cells makes Ewing sarcoma the overwhelming leading diagnosis.

DIAGNOSIS: Ewing sarcoma
